name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO)
summary: A heavyweight Mars orbiter with a 3 m dish and six science instruments, including a high-resolution camera, built to return huge volumes of data.
outcome: Reached Mars on 10 March 2006, aerobraked for six months into a 255 × 320 km science orbit and kept working through multiple mission extensions.
funFact: Its orbit-insertion burn lasted 27 minutes and slowed it by about 1 km/s. Six months of skimming the atmosphere did the rest.
notes: NSSDCA Master Catalog 2005-029A: maximum mass 2,180 kg including 1,149 kg of propellant; two 10 m² arrays producing 1,000 W at Mars; maximum data rate 6 Mbps; six science instruments; Atlas V 401; total cost estimated at about $720 million (the page gives no cost year: costYear is the launch year). primaryMissionYears is our scenario's value.

name: Juno
summary: A spinning, solar-powered Jupiter orbiter that dives beneath the radiation belts every perijove, with its electronics inside a titanium vault.
outcome: Arrived on 5 July 2016 after an Earth flyby. Its engine valves misbehaved, so it stayed in its 53-day orbit instead of moving to a 14-day one, and still completed its science.
funFact: Juno's three solar wings span about 20 m. They make 18 kW near Earth but only about 400 W at Jupiter.
notes: NSSDCA Master Catalog 2011-040A: Atlas V 551, Earth flyby 9 Oct 2013, orbit insertion 5 July 2016 into a 53.5-day orbit, 150 kg titanium vault, arrays give 18 kW at Earth and 400 W initially at Jupiter, mass 1,500 kg. JPL press kit: 3,625 kg at launch, nine instruments, about $1.1 billion. JPL release 'NASA's Juno to Remain in Current Orbit at Jupiter' (Feb 2017) for the valve decision. The array area in powerSource is approximate.

name: Lunar Prospector
summary: A small, low-cost spin-stabilised orbiter that mapped the Moon's composition, gravity and magnetic fields from a low polar orbit.
outcome: Its neutron spectrometer found extra hydrogen at both lunar poles, a sign of water ice in permanently shadowed craters. The mission ended on 31 July 1999.
funFact: Its last act was a deliberate crash into a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole, hoping to kick up water vapour. No plume was seen.
notes: NSSDCA Master Catalog 1998-001A: 296.4 kg fully fuelled with 137.7 kg of hydrazine (dry 158.7 kg), nominal power 202 W, six experiments, Athena 2, 100 km polar mapping orbit with a 118-minute period, total cost $62.8 million, launched 7 Jan 1998, ended 31 July 1999. Hydrogen result: NSSDCA 'Lunar Prospector Science Results'.
